reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: A variable-vessel vasculitis defined clinically by recurrent oral aphthous ulceration together with other features, as there is no specific diagnostic test
Recurrent painful genital ulcers and skin lesions such as erythema nodosum and pseudofolliculitis are characteristic
Ocular disease, particularly relapsing posterior uveitis and retinal vasculitis, is a major cause of vision loss
Pathergy (a papulo-pustular skin reaction to needle prick) supports the diagnosis where present
It is more prevalent along the historical Silk Road and is associated with HLA-B51
Vascular involvement is distinctive in affecting both arteries and veins, causing venous thromboses and arterial aneurysms, including pulmonary artery aneurysms
Neurological (neuro-Behçet) and gastrointestinal involvement carry significant morbidity
Treatment is tailored to organ involvement, using colchicine and topical measures for mucocutaneous disease and systemic immunosuppression or biologics for major organ threat
reference.pathophysiology: Behçet disease is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder classified as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can affect vessels of any size and type, both arterial and venous. Its cause is uncertain but involves genetic susceptibility (notably HLA-B51) and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity with prominent neutrophil hyperactivity, elevated Th1/Th17 responses, and inflammation triggered in predisposed individuals. Vascular inflammation produces thrombosis, aneurysm formation, and tissue damage, while immune-mediated inflammation drives the recurrent mucocutaneous, ocular, neurological, and gastrointestinal lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis without systemic disease
Inflammatory bowel disease with oral and skin manifestations
Herpes simplex and other infective causes of genital ulceration
Sarcoidosis and other causes of uveitis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment against recognised diagnostic/classification criteria (no confirmatory laboratory test)
Ophthalmological examination for uveitis and retinal vasculitis
Vascular imaging for venous thrombosis and arterial aneurysms, including pulmonary vessels
MRI brain and cerebrospinal fluid analysis when neuro-Behçet is suspected; HLA-B51 typing as supportive
redFlags: Sudden or progressive visual loss from posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis requiring urgent ophthalmology and immunosuppression
Neurological deficits (brainstem or cerebral involvement) or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis indicating neuro-Behçet
Pulmonary artery aneurysm presenting with haemoptysis, a life-threatening complication
Major vessel thrombosis or arterial aneurysm at risk of rupture
Severe gastrointestinal ulceration with bleeding or perforation
reference.prognosis: Course is relapsing and remitting and tends to be more severe in young men. Mucocutaneous disease is troublesome but not dangerous, whereas ocular, neurological, and major vascular involvement drive the risk of blindness, disability, and death. Early aggressive treatment of organ-threatening disease improves outcome.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent oral ulcers in isolation and missing systemic Behçet disease
Delaying immunosuppression for eye involvement and risking irreversible vision loss
Managing vascular thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without addressing the underlying inflammation, and overlooking coexisting aneurysms
Attributing neurological symptoms to other causes rather than neuro-Behçet
Assuming absence of pathergy or HLA-B51 excludes the diagnosis
management: Control recurrent oral and genital aphthous ulcers with topical corticosteroids and colchicine, adding apremilast for refractory oral ulceration
Treat arthritis and erythema nodosum with colchicine, using short corticosteroid courses or azathioprine for persistent disease

Manage relapsing posterior uveitis and retinal vasculitis aggressively with systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppression (azathioprine or ciclosporin), escalating to infliximab, adalimumab or interferon-alpha to preserve vision

Treat major vascular disease, including venous thrombosis and arterial or pulmonary artery aneurysms, with corticosteroids and immunosuppression such as cyclophosphamide or anti-TNF therapy rather than relying on anticoagulation
Manage neuro-Behcet with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, avoiding ciclosporin owing to neurotoxicity
Treat gastrointestinal involvement with corticosteroids, aminosalicylates and azathioprine or anti-TNF agents, with surgery for perforation or uncontrolled bleeding
Provide multidisciplinary follow-up and escalate immunosuppression promptly for organ- or sight-threatening disease, which runs a more severe course in young men

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Behcet disease

nodes.text: Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers with genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye or vascular features
Red flag: visual loss, neuro deficits, pulmonary artery aneurysm, major thrombosis or GI bleeding?
Escalate urgently to ophthalmology, neurology and vascular teams; start immunosuppression
Assess against classification criteria; pathergy test where available
Eye examination, vascular imaging; MRI brain and CSF if neuro-Behcet is suspected
Clinical criteria met? (no confirmatory laboratory test exists)
Treat by organ: topical steroids and colchicine for mucocutaneous disease
No: stays unconfirmed; HLA-B51 and pathergy alone do not settle the diagnosis
Systemic steroids with azathioprine or ciclosporin for uveitis; anti-TNF if refractory
Relapsing course; organ-threatening disease needs early escalation
